entities.summary:
Charles Malo François Lameth (1757–1832) was a prominent French aristocrat, military officer, and politician whose career spanned the tumultuous decades from the Ancien Régime through the French Revolution, Napoleonic Empire, and Bourbon Restoration. Born into a distinguished noble family in Paris, he was one of three influential Lameth brothers who collectively played a significant role in the early phases of the French Revolution. His trajectory, marked by initial revolutionary fervor for constitutional monarchy, subsequent emigration, and later service to imperial and restored royal regimes, encapsulates the complex political metamorphoses of late 18th and early 19th-century France. He is significant for his involvement in the foundational debates of the National Constituent Assembly and for embodying the adaptive pragmatism required for survival during an era of profound societal upheaval.

After serving with distinction in the American Revolutionary War alongside Lafayette, Lameth was elected as a deputy of the nobility for Péronne to the Estates-General in 1789. There, he quickly aligned with liberal nobles, joining the Breton Club and advocating for radical reforms such as the abolition of aristocratic privileges and the establishment of a constitutional monarchy. He played a key role in the National Constituent Assembly, notably supporting the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and advocating for the abolition of hereditary nobility in June 1790. His early revolutionary zeal, however, waned as the Revolution grew more radical; after the flight to Varennes and the Champ de Mars massacre in 1791, he fled France, fearing for his life, and spent several years in exile, primarily in Hamburg.
